title: Towards a Participatory Buddhism, Part 1
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett reads the first part of Carl Bielefeldt's essay on participatory Buddhism, which names five trends in American Buddhism: secularism, individualism, eclecticism, egalitarianism, and activism. Before reading, Nomon sits with news of the shooting at Freeman High School near Spokane, where a student who confronted the shooter was killed, and offers a minute of silence. Nomon then gives each trend a local example. A student in a mindfulness class asks to "have joy" instead of studying suffering, and white and black slippers at a Japanese training monastery show how rank works there. The essay's answer, Dogen's participatory Buddhism, waits for next week.

So first, some sad news.

It's hard.
It's hard to bear.

But somehow this one really touched me, so I want to share it and invite us to be with this one.
There was a school shooting in Spokane this afternoon in a small high school called Freeman High School.
Here's the news article.
*One person was killed and three were injured following a shooting at a high school near Spokane, Washington, officials said Wednesday.
One person died at Freeman High School while three injured victims were taken to the hospital.
The shooter is in custody, according to Spokane County Sheriff Ozzy Knasevich.
The student was killed, according to KREM, the student who was killed, was shot after confronting the shooter.
The suspected shooter apparently had two weapons and the first one jammed, at which point he was confronted by the student.
He then proceeded to shoot three other students before being detained by a staff member.
The three pediatric patients injured in the incident are currently in satisfactory condition, Sacred Heart Hospital told Fox News.*
*The shooter, quote, the shooter has been apprehended and taken into custody with law enforcement, an official said during a news conference following the incident.
There were initial reports of multiple shooters that wound up being false, the official said.
The suspect's identity and motive was not immediately known.
The three victims that survived are all stable and doing well, although one will need surgery later on Wednesday.*
It's probably happening right now.

A parent of a freshman at the school said her son called her from a classroom after hearing the shots fired.
"He called me and said, Mom, there's gunshots.
He sounded so scared.
I've never heard him like that," Cheryl Moser told the Spokane Review.
"You never think about things happening like this at a small school."*
*Stephanie Luce said she was relieved to hear her son was safe after his high school near Freeman was put on lockdown.
And she commended the school district for its communication with parents.
"It's amazing," she said.
"Within probably 15 or 20 minutes of hearing about it, I'd already received a phone call that he was okay, and I'd already received a text message saying that their school was okay."
Neighboring school districts, including Central Valley and Spokane Public, initially imposed lockdowns as precaution in reaction to the incident.
Freeman High School has more than 300 students according to the Spokane Review.*

*Governor Jay Inslee said in a statement that all Washingtonians are thinking of the victims and their families and are grateful for the service of school staff and first responders working to keep our students safe.
Senator Patty Murray said, "Heartbreaking headlines out of Spokane County.
My thoughts are with students, teachers, parents, first responders, and the entire community."*
So I thought we could bring that up and just sit with that for a minute.
That this happened.
An impressive amount of stuff.
Sounds like it went well, like the response was effective and clear.
And that here's this courageous teenager, and having a teenage boy myself, I think about this, at the school, who saw this moment that maybe he could make a difference.
Who paid for the safety of others with his life.
So let's just offer a minute for the suffering and the courage and the confusion and the coming together and the all of it that happens in that incident and all the time, really.
All right, thank you very much.
Maybe once that boy's name is released, we'll put his name on the altar.
So what I was really intending to talk about was some reflections on this American Zen experiment that we seem to be in the middle of.
But we don't always get to choose what we talk about, do we?
It's not up to us.
But we've got some time left, so we'll talk about that a little bit.
Now, we're actually in the middle of a pretty radical and, in some ways organic, in some ways deliberate, in some ways unexamined, experiment in a certain way of being.
A certain way of being in our own skin, being in our minds, being with each other.
Somehow circumstances and all kinds of weird stuff have happened, so that we're all sitting here in this room.
A group with some kind of continuity has been doing this weekly without fail for 26, 27 years.
So what are we actually doing?
What does it mean to say this is a Soto Zen sitting group and that we're a Sangha and that we're practicing?
So I want to share with you a really interesting essay by the American Buddhist scholar Carl Bielefeld, who's a faculty member at Stanford.
Our dear colleague Susan Elbe sent us this on the email.
Dr.
Bielefeld is part of a group, not a very big group, a small group of American-born scholars who just somehow had the right support, and somehow the academic institutions are still functional enough.
But this group of people really have dug deep into Buddhism, and particularly I'm thinking of a group that works in Japanese Buddhism and Zen Buddhism.
And the cool thing about this group, Carl Bielefeld and his colleagues, is that they also practice.

So they're on the one hand scholarly adepts who understand the historical significance of things and the context of things, and all of them can read some of the source languages, so they're reading some of these texts in the original.
In fact, this essay I want to read to you was also published in Japanese by Dr.
Bielefeld in the Japanese Buddhist Journal.
So he did the Japanese version and the English version.
Imagine that.
Wouldn't that be cool to do?

So these scholars, I think, are really helpful to us because they're sympathetic, because they have felt something in their own hearts around the value of practice, but they also retain a critical perspective and a broader understanding of where all this came from.
And I always feel like it's good to maintain multiple layers of truth around this.
There's a kind of historic truth that these guys are experts in.
What does this mean?
What was the context in which it emerged?
Chris gave us a great little background on Dogen's context in the 13th century.
So there's a kind of historic truth that matters.
But there's also a religious or devotional truth, that this really did come to us hand to hand, one person to the next, over 2600 years from the Buddha himself or herself.
And there's also a practical truth: how is this helpful to me?
How do I actually work with this?
How does this show up when I'm grouchy on the road or dealing with my difficult relative?
So I think it's nice that we have some reflections from these scholars, because they also exist in all these realms.
And Dr.

Bielenfeld makes some interesting observations about our cultural assumptions and our American predilections that may have slipped into Japanese Zen practice, in some ways for the better and maybe in some ways for not so much the better: that without completely meaning to, we've reinvented what Zen is or created a new form of Zen.
And of course, Buddhism is famous for adapting and changing as it reaches different cultures.
So Dr.
Bielenfeld makes some interesting specific points in this essay.
I'll just read the first part of it, make a few comments, and then next week maybe we'll hear the rest of it.
And I'll post the whole thing on the website too so you can read this for yourself.
So here's Dr.
Bielenfeld talking now.
*In October 1999, the Soto School held a celebration at Stanford of the 800th anniversary of Dogen's birth.*
Japanese love stuff like that.
Every anniversary for hundreds, thousands of years will be celebrated.
So this is the 800th anniversary of his birth.
*And on that occasion, I gave a talk entitled "Living with Dogen: Thoughts on the Relevance of His Thought."
The talk concerned issues in Dogen's religious thought that I felt will need to be addressed if we were to formulate a contemporary version of Dogen's Zen.

My purpose was simply to lay out certain historical characteristics of Dogen's approach to Zen, and I dealt only in passing with the contemporary scene and did not try to imagine the shape of a contemporary Buddhism.
Nevertheless, at the end of my talk, I did suggest one general feature of Dogen's approach to Zen that I thought might be especially relevant to a modern rethinking of Zen religious life.
I called that feature participatory Buddhism.*
Participatory Buddhism.
*And here, in this essay, I would like to pursue this notion a bit and see if I can relate it to issues facing the contemporary Buddhist community.
Let me begin with several caveats.*
I like to start my talk with caveats.
So I like that.
*First, I am by training an historian of Buddhism, not a theologian and not a sociologist of contemporary religion.
Thus, I have no particular expertise in my subject matter here.
I am speaking only as a Buddhist lay person interested in the future of the religion, and I hope that specialists in my subject matter here will sharpen my ideas and correct my mistakes.
Second, I am speaking as an American Buddhist layman about issues in the American community.
I leave it to others more better qualified to decide whether and how what I say here is relevant to Buddhism in Japan.
Third, and speaking of the American community, I have in mind only the Buddhism found in American converts to the religion, not the religion of the Nikkei and other ethnic communities.*
Nikkei means the second and third generation of Japanese Americans, because those have their own distinctive characteristics.
So he's talking about us guys.

*Finally, I should warn the reader at the start that my thoughts here are those of a religious and political liberal who has doubts about much in both the traditional and the current interpretations of Buddhism.*
So then he has a section header, American Buddhism, and he goes on.
*If you want to become a Buddhist, you have to come into conversation with American Buddhism.

I see at least five trends that tend to distinguish this Buddhism from traditional forms in Asia, trends that in one form or another have been noted by others as well in recent studies of the American Buddhist scene.
I call these five trends secularism, eclecticism, egalitarianism, and activism.*
He's going to go through these: secularism, individualism, eclecticism, egalitarianism, and activism.
Now he's going to go through them one at a time, and I'll summarize them again at the end.

*By secularism, I mean a tendency of a peculiar feature of modernity to view the sacred realm of religion as a product of human culture rather than viewing the worlds of nature and culture as the expression of a sacred realm.*
Do you want to hear that again?
*I mean a tendency often identified as a peculiar feature of modernity to view the sacred realm of religion rather than viewing the worlds of nature and culture as the expression of a sacred realm.
American Buddhists do not typically see their country as a mandala, which was a traditional Buddhist sense.*
*Your country is a mandala.
We don't see our country as a mandala.
Americans do not read their history as stages of the Dharma leading to the coming of Maitreya.
They do not see their own lives as preparation for rebirth They do not treat the ideas and practices of Buddhism as manifestations of the Dharmakaya.
Rather, Buddhism is but one human option in a world of many options and it must compete in the marketplace to prove its value both to the individual and to society.
Like any product on the market, Buddhism can manipulate the taste of its consumers through skillful advertising but it must also cater to their taste through skillful packaging.*
That sounds a little more negative than I think he quite means, so hang in there.
He's very respectful of this actually, but he's noticing something.
So, secularism: seeing the sacred as created by our choices and actions.
I'm not inherently already here.
*By individualism, I mean a tendency to treat Buddhism as a vehicle for personal experience rather than a religious institution or a social community or a cultural tradition.
Americans today often make a sharp distinction between religion and spirituality.
The former having to do with institution, ritual and dogma, the latter concerned with an individual's inner life.
In this distinction, religion is seen as somewhat suspect, as shallow and inauthentic.
Spirituality is seen as pure and beautiful.

Although the language of spirituality often puts great value on a common humanity and a harmony between the human and natural worlds, it's typically concerned first and foremost with private experience.
How do I feel about myself and humanity and the world?*
Or what has been called idolatry, like capital I.
Idolatry.
A fetish of me, you know.
*For many American Buddhists, then, membership in a Buddhist organization is a secondary concern.
An acceptance of the norms of a particular Buddhist community is as much a compromise as it is a commitment.*
So we kind of stick making our own experience primary.
Third thing he talks about, more secularism than individualism, now eclecticism.
I don't know if that's an actual word or if you made that up, eclecticism.
So, being eclectic.

*By eclecticism, I mean the tendency to shop around in the religious marketplace for what is attractive and to put together a personal view of spirituality that may be drawn from a variety of sources, both Buddhist and non-Buddhist.

There's a great variety of options, both imported forms of the religion from virtually all the countries of Asia and new domestic forms of mixed traditional Buddhist teachings with elements drawn from psychology, new age spirituality, ecology, and other current enthusiasms.
In such a marketplace, it's hardly surprising that Americans, suspicious as they are of church dogma, tend to show very little brand loyalty for a particular tradition.
Sectarian identity is a fairly fluid matter and a mix of Buddhist sources, from Dogen to Thich Nhat Hanh to the Dalai Lama, it's fairly common.
The various traditions of Asian Buddhism are kind of like imported natural resources to be fashioned into finished products by the American spiritual industry.*
So that's eclecticism, being eclectic, pulling different things together.
I think it's a little tongue-in-cheek, but I think as you hear this there's a little part of you that goes, "Yeah, I do that."
Okay.
Not that bad, though.
Okay, next is egalitarianism.
*By egalitarianism, I mean the tendency to imagine that each individual is an equal player in spiritual life.

To be sure, in its formative period, American Buddhism has seen its share of what is sometimes called guru worship, but there is a deeper cultural habit of resistance to authority and resentment of hierarchy.
The spiritual superiority of the Buddhist clergy is suspect.
The wisdom of the elders needs to be demonstrated.
The authority granted to Asian teachers is continually undercut by a sense of American spirit*
I haven't seen that so much.

*Deference to those deeply steeped in Buddhist tradition is weakened by a youth culture that values what is new and original and leadership in the communities by consensus to be arrived at democratically.
Men cannot speak for women, women speak for themselves, and demand a Buddhism that speaks to them as women.*
*Finally, by activism, I mean a tendency to think of Buddhism as a practice rather than as a belief system or a world that you can inhabit.

There are, of course, many Americans who simply appreciate Buddhism as a worldview or a way of thinking about things, and many who describe their beliefs and themselves as Buddhists, but do nothing about it.
Yet Americans seem drawn to Buddhism as something to do and as a set of therapeutic spiritual exercises that can be engaged in.
They may have little fondness for church dogma and ritual, but they have faith in the goal of enlightenment and the practices supposed to bring it about.
Hence American lay people are not content to leave meditation to the monks.
They want to be involved in spiritual training themselves.
As a refuge from problems, they expect the religion to solve problems.
Not only their own personal problems, but the problems of the world.
War, social injustice, environmental degradation, and the like.
They want to use their religion to make spiritual and sometimes even material progress.
And they measure the value of their religion by its results.*
So here's his critique.
We don't need to get defensive or anything.
He's not saying this is bad.
He's saying that we need a day like this and see how to dance with it.
So let's just run through it one more time: secularism, individualism, eclecticism, egalitarianism, and activism.
So, secularism, putting less of an emphasis on sort of an essential sacredness.
Secularism and practice and the spiritual life as a way to express that and feel it and know it in a deep way.
And have faith in it, whether you feel it or not.
So instead of that, to feel like practice creates environments and creates situations where we touch the sacred and we feel the sacred.
You hang around a sesshin for enough days you feel like, "Oh good, we're getting there."
Individualism: approaching what we're doing as separate individuals, not merging completely with the community.
We ask how I want to practice.
We don't ask how are we practicing.
Eclecticism, putting our own eclectic collection of beliefs and practices together.
A little this, a little that.
This morning I was giving a little talk to a mindfulness group about Buddhism.
This is my new thing, teaching Buddhism to non-Buddhists.
It's really fun.
And so I was talking about dukkha, talking about suffering and a bunch of other stuff.
Talking about the three marks of existence and the six paramitas and all that.
And one of them raised his hand and said, "Let's have joy."
And he was very serious and I agreed with him in a way.
He said, "Let's have joy instead.
Let's focus on joy.
Let's have all these wonderful practices and understand what you're talking about.
We don't need to focus on suffering, we need joy."
But that's exactly that, right, isn't it?
That's eclecticism.
And I've got a reason for that.
What was that?
Yeah.
So, activism, egalitarianism.
So we're all equal.
And here I feel like we're always kind of playing with balancing between a sort of horizontalness.
That yes, we are all equal, true enough.
Nobody has a corner on the special soup or something.
We're all just human beings, and so we try to practice egalitarianism.
But then we've recognized over time that trying to only do that basically is really bad.
Trying to do pure egalitarianism ends up with the opposite result of what you wanted.
Everybody feels oppressed.
Everybody feels like nobody's allowed to have a voice.
So we recognize over time you need a certain amount of verticality and depth of training and different ranks and all this stuff.
And that helps us too.
But we let the two of them reflect on each other.
So egalitarianism, that we're all equal, is just that sort of side of it.
So hopefully we balance that okay here.
Who knows?
Every one of us has a different relationship to all this, right?
And we all are different about how we think it's supposed to be because we have individualism too, right?
So it's a funny mix that you could only have this certain flavor of egalitarianism with individualism, right?
If you didn't have individualism, why would you worry about it, you know?
You just merge with the collective.

And then finally, activism is interesting because we're talking about it not just as activism, like political activism, like we've been a little more involved in since things happened, but activism as a sort of more fundamental idea: activism as the belief that activity results in something.
So activism, like action-vism.
That the application and purposeful practice of something, Buddhism, leads to a particular result that is desirable to us.
But it also includes political activism.
But that's an extension of the same idea, is what he's saying.
And an activist side note: I ran into some people from community to community today who are picketing in front of the courthouse.
And I asked them about our Mexican colleagues who got fired from the Cerebon Farms and they said they're all either in Mexico or on their way.
And that's all worked out.
But they said, but there's still 300 people working at Cerebon Farms under the same visa restrictions and the same working conditions.
So they said, "We're not stopping.
We got through a crisis, but we're not stopping."
So anyway.
So all of this is really different from how Dogen students probably perceive practice.
Not that they didn't have elements of all this.
These are human things.
They're not merely cultural, but they are also quite cultural.
So the suggestion here is that Dogen students in the 13th century had much more of a sense of sort of being immersed and steeped in the sacred.
They had much less of a sense of themselves as a separate individual doing actions to lead to a result.
That the practice is an expression of Buddha, not formation of Buddha.
And this is a very non-egalitarian culture, so maybe it didn't occur to anybody to question authority or anything like that.
And those of us who have been to the great training monasteries in Japan in recent days have seen that, of course, the system of a very strong verticality is still practiced there.
Did I tell you about the slipper colors before?
The slipper colors.
So the usual stint at AHG is two years.
I might have the colors reversed, but something like this.
Year one, when you're cruising around in the long hallways of AHG, you wear white slippers.
Year two, you wear black slippers.
So if you're in a white slipper crew and you're trying to get from point A to point B and a group of black slipper people comes along, you stop.
And you bow.
And you wait.
And you wait.
And you wait.
Well, they go by.
Well, they go by.
Well, they go by.
So, you know, not egalitarian.
It's not even kind.
Everything's ranked and everybody's aware of where they are in the hierarchy and their particular practices.
They're very depending on where you are in that hierarchy.
And our colleagues, actually, I quite love our colleagues at Dharma Rains and Community in Portland.
What a wonderful center.
But their teacher, G.U.
Kennett, inherited that system, too, and kind of passed it on to them.
So they talk there about juniors and seniors.
You know, respecting your seniors and juniors knowing their place and stuff like that.
You know, the first time I heard that, like, "What did you just say?
Juniors?
Seniors?
Is this high school?"
Yeah.
But there's a kind of beauty to that, too, you know.
The beauty of knowing your place, you know.
Very powerful.
So, Dr.
Bielefeld has set this up, and he'll pay it off for us next week, or in the meantime.
You can read this yourself, if I remember to email it to you.
That there's some value both to our American sensibilities and to Dogen's, you know, our understanding from this vantage point of how Dogen understood practice.
And that Dogen introduced a particular sensibility to practice, you know, or reinforced one that was already there that he calls participatory Buddhism.
That can be kind of a bridge between the traditional Asian understanding and our American can-do attitude.
So that will come later.
All right?
So thanks for listening to this talk and many, many talks before, and many talks to come if we don't all fall over.
And speaking of all falling over, Hannah was telling me she's working on the project of helping us define and understand end-of-life concerns, which no matter what age you are, we all should have.
And so there will be some workshops and stuff around how to define your wishes, medical funeral wishes, and all that stuff, because it's just a matter of time, right?
No, yeah, but joy, it's just joyful.
Death is joyful.
We like death.
Go death.
Yeah.
Life is, can't have life without death, man.
Can't have death without life.
So we spend a lot of time on life, so let's spend a lot on death.
So anyway, that will be a wonderful announcement.

She and her colleagues, you know, and we're blessed by having several medical professions amongst the sangha, you know, so they're already educated about all this stuff and can help us sort of understand what we would want to have ready, you know, before this stuff happens, and it could happen tomorrow, we don't know.
So there's that.
May our intentions be believed.
